eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 2, Lesson 9
subtitle: A detector that's 95% accurate flags fraud only ~19% of the time. Here's why.

code:
P(H | E) = P(E | H) * P(H) / P(E)

# Prior P(H):      belief before the evidence (the base rate)
# Likelihood P(E|H): how likely the evidence is if H is true
# Posterior P(H|E):  the updated belief -- what we want
caption: Derived from writing P(A and B) two ways and setting them equal.

code:
p_fraud, sens, fpr = 0.005, 0.95, 0.02
p_flag = sens * p_fraud + fpr * (1 - p_fraud)
post = sens * p_fraud / p_flag
print(p_flag, post)
# 0.02465  0.1927
caption: 2.465% of transactions get flagged -- but only ~19.3% of flagged ones are actually fraud.

code:
# 100,000 transactions:
# 500 fraud      -> detector catches 475 (95%)
# 99,500 legit   -> detector flags 1,990 anyway (2%)
# truly fraud of those flagged: 475 / 2,465 = 19.3%
caption: A tiny 2% false-positive rate, times a huge legitimate majority, swamps the true catches.

code:
fraud = rng.random(n) < 0.005
flag = np.where(fraud, rng.random(n) < 0.95, rng.random(n) < 0.02)
print(fraud[flag].mean())   # 0.1921 -- close to the exact 0.1927
caption: The base rate fallacy: ignoring how rare fraud is leads to over-trusting a positive flag.

eyebrow: The same detector, different base rates
code:
# prior 0.1%  -> posterior  4.5%
# prior 0.5%  -> posterior 19.3%
# prior   5%  -> posterior 71.4%
# prior  20%  -> posterior 92.2%
caption: Nearly useless on rare events, quite strong on common ones -- accuracy alone can mislead.

eyebrow: Updating with a second, independent alert
code:
p2 = sens * post / (sens * post + fpr * (1 - post))
print(p2)   # 0.9189
caption: Yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior -- but only if the two alerts are truly independent.
